lesson.title: Jailbreaks: talking a chatbot round
lesson.subtitle: Why refusals leak, and what a school does about it

video.title: Jailbreaks: talking a chatbot round
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Cards: A proud screenshot; A cruel poem; “Just for a story”.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A pupil showed me a screenshot, very proud of himself. He had got a chatbot to write a cruel poem about a classmate. At first it refused, so he told it it was “just for a story”.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why chatbots can be talked round their rules, and what a school does about it.

scenes.visual: A list: Trained to refuse harm; Learned from examples; Says no to known wordings; New wordings may slip.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Chatbots are trained to refuse harmful requests. But that refusal is learned, like everything else the model does. It learned to say no to the kinds of wording it saw in training. A new wording may not trigger it.

scenes.visual: A list: Role play; “Only for a story”; Harmless-looking pieces; Another language; Many turns.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A jailbreak is an attempt to talk a chatbot round its safety rules. People try role play, “it's only for a story”, splitting a request into harmless-looking pieces, another language, or wearing it down over many turns.

scenes.visual: A list: Pupils swap tricks; Screenshots get shared; Your school's name on it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Why does this matter at school? Pupils swap tricks like these, and the results get screenshotted and shared. A chatbot on your school's website can be pushed into saying something harmful, with the school's name on it.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A chatbot refused a request, then answered when the same request was dressed up as a story. What does that show?

scenes.visual: Two columns. The model alone: Refuses known wordings; Misses new ones. Layers around it: Checks in code; People watching; Reports and fixes.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Its refusals are learned, so they don't cover every wording. That's no reason to give up on the model. It's a reason not to rely on the model alone.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Run a bank of requests; Count the refusals; Read what got through; Rate how bad, then fix.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Defenders test this on purpose, with permission. It's called red teaming: run a bank of requests the chatbot should refuse, count how many it does, and read the ones that got through. Each miss is a finding: what was tried, what got through, and how bad it is.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Six of eight, then eight of eight
scenes.narration: Our small model, Darsi Tiny, refused six of eight test requests in English, and seven in Arabic. A rule in code caught the rest: eight out of eight.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Run the bank; Read the misses; Add a rule in code; Run it again.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, run the bank against Darsi Tiny. Read each miss: what slipped through, and how bad it is. Then add a rule in code and run it again.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My pupils want a contest: who can get the class chatbot to say the rudest thing. What do I say?

scenes.visual: The summary: Refusals are learned; New wordings slip past; Layers, not the model alone; Test with permission, then fix. Takeaway: A refusal is a start, not a wall: build layers and report the gaps.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: No contests: report what slips through instead. Remember: refusals are learned, so new wordings can slip past. Don't rely on the model alone: layer filters, checks in code and people. And test on purpose, with permission, then fix.

scenes.visual: A list: Guard a harmless secret; Classmates reword politely; Count what slips past; Add a second keeper.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “The rule keeper”. One pupil guards a harmless secret, like the colour of a box, with one rule: never say it. Classmates try polite rewordings. Count what slips past, then add a second keeper who checks every answer.

checkpoints.prompt: A chatbot refused a request, then answered when the same request was dressed up as a story. What does that show?

options.text: The chatbot is broken and useless
Its refusals are learned and don't cover every wording
Stories are always safe to ask for

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: it learned to refuse certain wordings, and the story was a new one.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: it isn't broken. Its refusals are learned, so a new wording can slip past.

checkpoints.prompt: Pupils want a contest: who can get the class chatbot to say the rudest thing. What do you say?

options.text: “No contests on real services; report what slips through instead”

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: testing is for people with permission. Pupils report what they find.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a contest spreads harmful output and may break the service's rules. Report, don't compete.
